title: Acute Respiratory Failure: Oxygenation or Ventilation?
bottomLine: When breathing is failing, identify whether the dominant problem is oxygenation, ventilation, or both, stabilize immediately, and treat the cause. Do not wait for a perfect diagnosis before supporting airway and breathing.
recognize: Hypoxemic failure presents with inadequate oxygenation despite escalating oxygen; hypercapnic failure reflects inadequate alveolar ventilation and may cause headache, somnolence or altered mental status.
Work of breathing, fatigue, mental-status change and trajectory matter as much as a single oxygen saturation.
differentiate: Asthma/COPD, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, PE, pneumothorax, CNS depression and neuromuscular weakness produce different mechanisms.
A normal pulse oximeter does not exclude dangerous hypercapnia.
assessment: Assess airway patency, respiratory rate, effort, speech, mental status, oxygenation, circulation and likely reversible cause.
Look for silent chest, unilateral absent breath sounds, pulmonary edema, opioid/sedative exposure and neuromuscular weakness.
workup: Obtain blood gas when ventilation or acid-base status will change management; use chest imaging, ECG and targeted labs according to the suspected cause.
Do not delay decompression of a clinically unstable tension pneumothorax for imaging.
management: Position, oxygenate and escalate respiratory support according to severity; use non-invasive ventilation only when appropriate and the patient can protect the airway.
Arrange definitive airway management when ventilation, oxygenation, mental status or fatigue is worsening despite support.
medicationSafety: Treat bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, infection, overdose or anaphylaxis according to cause rather than giving sedatives for distress.
Excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible COPD patients, but clinically important hypoxemia must still be corrected.
counselling: Explain escalation in simple terms and involve substitute decision-makers when capacity is lost, without delaying emergency treatment.
followUp: After stabilization, reassess the precipitating cause, baseline lung disease, inhaler/medication access and recurrence prevention.
examTrap: Being reassured by a normal oxygen saturation in a somnolent patient with opioid toxicity or ventilatory failure.
oneLinePearl: Pulse oximetry measures oxygenation, not ventilation.

title: ABG and Acid-Base: Find the Primary Disorder
bottomLine: Interpret acid-base results in sequence: pH, primary respiratory versus metabolic process, expected compensation, then anion gap when metabolic acidosis is present. A mixed disorder is present when compensation is not appropriate for the primary process.
recognize: Respiratory disorders move pH opposite to PaCO2; metabolic disorders move pH with bicarbonate.
High-anion-gap acidosis should trigger a cause-focused search such as lactate, ketoacidosis, renal failure or toxins.
differentiate: Compensation does not normally overshoot into the opposite pH range.
A near-normal pH can hide two serious opposing disorders.
assessment: Interpret the gas in clinical context: ventilation, perfusion, glucose/ketones, renal function, medications/toxins, vomiting/diarrhea and sepsis risk.
workup: Calculate the anion gap when relevant and compare measured compensation with the expected physiologic response.
Trend blood gases only when the result will guide treatment or respiratory support.
management: Treat the cause rather than chasing the pH number: restore perfusion, ventilation, insulin when indicated, stop toxin exposure, or correct major electrolyte/volume losses.
Severe or rapidly worsening acidemia requires urgent escalation.
medicationSafety: Routine bicarbonate therapy is not a substitute for treating shock, DKA or ventilatory failure and may be harmful in some settings.
redFlags: Suspected toxic alcohol or salicylate exposure
counselling: For stable chronic disorders, explain the underlying disease and medication factors that can precipitate decompensation.
followUp: Repeat the relevant chemistry or gas after treatment when trajectory determines further intervention.
examTrap: Calling a normal pH normal acid-base status without checking PaCO2 and bicarbonate for a mixed disorder.
oneLinePearl: A normal pH does not rule out a dangerous mixed acid-base disorder.
sourceBasis: Canadian critical-care and emergency medicine practice principles

title: Hyperkalemia: Protect the Heart First
bottomLine: True severe hyperkalemia or hyperkalemia with ECG toxicity is an emergency. Confirm that the sample is not spuriously elevated when clinically appropriate, but do not delay cardiac stabilization when the patient is high risk or the ECG is abnormal.
recognize: Risk is increased by CKD/AKI, potassium supplements, RAAS blockade, mineralocorticoid antagonists, trimethoprim, metabolic acidosis and tissue breakdown.
ECG changes can progress from peaked T waves and conduction slowing to sine-wave rhythm and arrest, but a normal ECG does not guarantee safety.
differentiate: Hemolyzed specimens can cause pseudohyperkalemia; thrombocytosis or extreme leukocytosis can also distort results.
The urgency is determined by potassium level, trajectory, renal function, symptoms and ECG—not by one number alone.
assessment: Assess weakness, palpitations, renal function, urine output, medications, supplements, recent illness and tissue injury.
Obtain an ECG promptly when clinically significant hyperkalemia is suspected.
workup: Repeat potassium if pseudohyperkalemia is plausible and the patient is stable; assess creatinine, bicarbonate, glucose and contributing abnormalities.
management: Use IV calcium for membrane stabilization when ECG toxicity or severe instability is present, then shift potassium intracellularly and remove potassium from the body using the appropriate acute-care pathway.
Stop contributors and involve nephrology/critical care when refractory or dialysis may be required.
medicationSafety: Insulin used to shift potassium can cause hypoglycemia, so glucose monitoring is mandatory.
Do not resume potassium-raising drugs until the cause and recurrence risk are addressed.
counselling: Review hidden potassium sources, salt substitutes and medication interactions after stabilization.
followUp: Recheck potassium after temporizing therapy because intracellular shifting is temporary and rebound can occur.
examTrap: Treating insulin as definitive potassium removal and failing to plan elimination or repeat testing.
oneLinePearl: Calcium protects the myocardium; shifting therapies buy time; potassium still has to leave the body.
sourceBasis: Kidney Foundation of Canada clinical resources

title: Sodium Emergencies: Treat Symptoms and Tempo
bottomLine: Sodium disorders are brain-risk disorders. Severe neurologic symptoms require urgent controlled treatment, while over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia or hypernatremia can itself cause catastrophic neurologic injury.
recognize: Hyponatremia may cause headache, nausea, confusion, seizures or coma; hypernatremia often reflects water deficit and can also cause neurologic dysfunction.
The same sodium value has different risk depending on how quickly it developed.
differentiate: Hyponatremia requires assessment of tonicity and volume status; hyperglycemia can lower measured sodium without true hypotonic hyponatremia.
SIADH is a diagnosis reached after considering volume status and excluding important mimics such as adrenal insufficiency.
assessment: Assess neurologic status, duration, fluid losses/intake, medications, kidney/heart/liver disease, endocrine symptoms and volume status.
workup: Use serum osmolality, urine osmolality and urine sodium when they will clarify hypotonic hyponatremia; assess glucose, renal function and endocrine causes as indicated.
management: Seizures or severe symptoms from hyponatremia require urgent hypertonic-saline management in a monitored setting.
Correct chronic sodium abnormalities at a controlled rate and address the cause rather than normalizing the number rapidly.
medicationSafety: Thiazides, SSRIs/SNRIs, carbamazepine and other drugs can contribute to hyponatremia.
Desmopressin and fluid strategies require close monitoring when used to control correction.
counselling: Explain fluid recommendations precisely; generic advice to drink more water can worsen some hyponatremic states.
followUp: Trend sodium frequently during active correction and arrange cause-specific follow-up after stabilization.
examTrap: Correcting chronic hyponatremia to normal as fast as possible.
oneLinePearl: With sodium, the speed of change can be as dangerous as the value.

title: Calcium Disorders: Symptoms, ECG, and Cause
bottomLine: Confirm clinically important calcium abnormalities with albumin-aware interpretation or ionized calcium when needed, then decide urgency from symptoms, ECG effects, renal function and severity. Always look for the cause rather than treating the number in isolation.
recognize: Hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, constipation, kidney stones, weakness, cognitive change and arrhythmia; malignancy and hyperparathyroidism are important causes.
Hypocalcemia can cause paresthesias, tetany, seizures and QT prolongation.
differentiate: Total calcium can mislead when albumin is abnormal; ionized calcium is more direct when accuracy is critical.
Magnesium deficiency can make hypocalcemia difficult to correct.
assessment: Review malignancy symptoms, supplements, thiazides/lithium, CKD, neck surgery, vitamin D exposure and volume status.
workup: Use PTH as the key branch point in persistent hypercalcemia; assess phosphate, magnesium, renal function and vitamin D according to the pattern.
management: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia requires monitored rehydration and cause-specific acute therapy; symptomatic hypocalcemia may require IV calcium.
Treat the underlying endocrine, renal, malignant or medication cause.
medicationSafety: Calcium and vitamin D supplements are not harmless in hypercalcemia or certain granulomatous diseases.
Lithium and thiazides can contribute to hypercalcemia.
counselling: Review supplements and over-the-counter products explicitly.
followUp: Persistent abnormalities require cause-specific endocrine/nephrology follow-up rather than repeated empiric supplementation.
examTrap: Calling elevated total calcium true hypercalcemia without considering albumin or ionized calcium when the context makes total calcium unreliable.
oneLinePearl: PTH tells you whether persistent hypercalcemia is parathyroid-driven.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism resources

title: Magnesium Disorders: Think Arrhythmia and Refractory Electrolytes
bottomLine: Low magnesium can promote ventricular arrhythmias and make potassium or calcium abnormalities refractory to treatment. High magnesium is usually a renal-clearance or iatrogenic problem and can cause weakness, hyporeflexia and cardiorespiratory depression.
recognize: Hypomagnesemia is associated with diarrhea, diuretics, alcohol use, PPIs and poor intake.
Hypermagnesemia is most concerning in renal impairment or after large magnesium exposure.
differentiate: Persistent hypokalemia despite replacement should trigger a magnesium check.
Neuromuscular depression with renal failure and magnesium-containing products should raise concern for hypermagnesemia.
assessment: Review GI losses, diuretics, PPI use, alcohol, kidney function and supplements/antacids/laxatives.
workup: Check potassium, calcium, renal function and ECG when the abnormality is clinically significant.
management: Replace magnesium according to severity and symptoms; urgent IV therapy is appropriate for serious arrhythmia or severe symptomatic deficiency.
Stop magnesium exposure and escalate severe hypermagnesemia, especially with renal failure.
medicationSafety: Renal impairment increases risk from magnesium-containing antacids/laxatives and IV replacement.
counselling: Ask patients to include supplements and laxatives when reporting medications.
followUp: Recheck associated potassium/calcium abnormalities after magnesium correction.
examTrap: Escalating potassium replacement repeatedly while missing concurrent magnesium deficiency.
oneLinePearl: Refractory potassium or calcium problems often have a magnesium problem underneath.

title: Volume Status and IV Fluids: Replace What Is Missing
bottomLine: IV fluid is a drug. Decide whether the patient needs resuscitation, replacement of ongoing losses, maintenance, or no additional fluid, then reassess response and stop when benefit is no longer evident.
recognize: Hypovolemia can cause tachycardia, orthostasis, poor perfusion, oliguria and prerenal kidney injury; fluid overload causes edema, elevated venous pressure and pulmonary congestion.
Older adults, heart failure, CKD and cirrhosis have a narrow margin between under- and over-resuscitation.
differentiate: Edema does not guarantee intravascular volume excess; cirrhosis and nephrotic states can have edema with reduced effective circulating volume.
A single blood pressure does not define fluid responsiveness.
assessment: Integrate history of losses/intake, vitals, perfusion, orthostasis when safe, JVP, lung findings, edema, urine output and weight trend.
workup: Use electrolytes, creatinine, urine output and focused ultrasound or dynamic assessments when they will change resuscitation decisions.
management: Use isotonic crystalloid for most initial volume resuscitation and reassess after each clinically meaningful intervention.
Treat hemorrhage with a blood-product strategy rather than endless crystalloid.
medicationSafety: Large unmonitored fluid volumes can worsen pulmonary edema, abdominal compartment pressure and dilutional abnormalities.
counselling: For chronic disease, explain daily weight and fluid/sodium plans only when indicated and individualized.
followUp: Reassess perfusion, lungs, urine output, electrolytes and cumulative balance.
examTrap: Continuing fluids because the patient was initially hypotensive even after signs of fluid intolerance appear.
oneLinePearl: Give fluid for a reason, measure the response, and stop when the reason is gone.

title: Transfusion Reactions: Stop the Blood First
bottomLine: New fever, dyspnea, hypotension, flank/back pain, urticaria or other concerning symptoms during transfusion are a transfusion reaction until assessed. Stop the transfusion, maintain IV access appropriately, stabilize the patient and notify the transfusion service according to local protocol.
recognize: Acute hemolytic reaction can cause fever, pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria and DIC; anaphylaxis causes airway/circulatory compromise; TRALI causes acute non-cardiogenic respiratory distress; TACO reflects circulatory overload.
differentiate: TRALI and TACO can both cause dyspnea and bilateral infiltrates but differ in volume status and mechanism.
Mild isolated urticaria is different from anaphylaxis, but airway symptoms or hypotension demand emergency treatment.
assessment: Stop the transfusion and assess ABCs, vitals, oxygenation, rash, lung findings, JVP/volume status and urine when relevant.
workup: Follow the institutional transfusion-reaction pathway, including clerical checks and blood-bank testing when indicated.
management: Provide cause-specific supportive treatment; use epinephrine promptly for anaphylaxis and diuresis for TACO when clinically appropriate.
Do not restart a stopped unit unless the reaction has been assessed and protocol explicitly permits it.
medicationSafety: Premedicating routinely does not prevent the most dangerous transfusion reactions and should not create false reassurance.
counselling: Explain the suspected reaction and document future transfusion precautions when applicable.
followUp: Ensure the reaction is documented and communicated to the transfusion service and future care teams.
examTrap: Slowing the transfusion and observing rather than stopping it when a serious reaction is suspected.
oneLinePearl: Suspected serious transfusion reaction: stop the blood before you sort out the subtype.
sourceBasis: Canadian Blood Services clinical transfusion resources

title: Shock: Identify the Failing Circulatory Mechanism
bottomLine: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion, not simply low blood pressure. Stabilize first while distinguishing hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic and obstructive mechanisms because the wrong resuscitation strategy can worsen the patient.
recognize: Shock may present with altered mentation, cool or mottled skin, oliguria, tachycardia, rising lactate and narrow pulse pressure; early distributive shock can be warm and vasodilated.
Obstructive causes include massive PE, tamponade and tension pneumothorax.
differentiate: Cardiogenic shock often has pulmonary congestion and pump failure; hypovolemic shock has low preload; distributive shock has pathologic vasodilation; obstructive shock blocks filling or outflow.
Normal blood pressure can coexist with compensated shock.
assessment: Assess ABCs, perfusion, mental status, capillary refill, skin temperature, JVP, lungs, bleeding, infection/anaphylaxis and point-of-care ultrasound when available and competent.
workup: Use ECG, lactate, CBC, chemistry, blood gas and targeted imaging/cultures based on the suspected mechanism, but do not delay life-saving treatment.
management: Control hemorrhage, give appropriate fluid/blood, use vasoactive support when indicated, treat sepsis/anaphylaxis, support pump failure and urgently relieve obstructive causes.
Reassess after every major intervention.
medicationSafety: Large empiric fluid loads can worsen cardiogenic shock; vasopressors given without addressing severe hypovolemia or obstruction may also fail.
redFlags: Evidence of major hemorrhage or obstruction
counselling: Communication with family should not delay resuscitation; provide updates as the mechanism becomes clearer.
followUp: After stabilization, identify the precipitating disease and monitor end-organ recovery.
examTrap: Defining shock by systolic blood pressure alone or giving the same fluid strategy to every shock state.
oneLinePearl: Shock is a perfusion diagnosis; mechanism determines treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian critical-care and emergency medicine practice principles

title: Clinical Deterioration: Escalate Before the Diagnosis Is Perfect
bottomLine: A worsening patient needs reassessment and escalation, not anchoring on the original diagnosis. Trend physiology, identify immediate threats, call for help early and communicate the change in condition clearly.
recognize: New oxygen requirement, rising respiratory rate, hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, severe pain out of proportion, rapidly changing labs or staff/family concern can precede arrest.
Trajectory is often more important than whether a single value has crossed a textbook cutoff.
differentiate: Expected illness symptoms should improve or remain physiologically stable; unexpected trajectory demands a fresh differential.
Do not dismiss deterioration as anxiety, age or baseline disability without reassessment.
assessment: Repeat ABCDE assessment, vital signs and focused exam; compare with the prior state and review recent medications/procedures and pending results.
workup: Order only tests that will rapidly clarify or change management while escalation is occurring.
management: Activate rapid response/emergency transfer according to setting, stabilize immediate threats and use structured handoff with the exact change, concern and requested action.
Revisit code status/goals of care when clinically appropriate, but do not infer treatment limits that have not been established.
medicationSafety: Check recent opioids, sedatives, insulin, anticoagulants, antihypertensives and other medications that can explain acute deterioration.
redFlags: Repeated clinician or family concern despite apparently normal numbers
counselling: Tell the patient/family that the condition has changed and what escalation is happening; use clear language without false reassurance.
followUp: Document the deterioration, response, handoff and responsibility for pending investigations.
examTrap: Waiting for confirmatory imaging or a consultant callback while the patient's physiology is getting worse.
oneLinePearl: When the trajectory worsens, reassess the patient—not the old diagnosis.
